extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory logic and set theory (mathematics or computer science)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, definitions, and reasoning techniques for sentential logic and basic set theory: identifying free/bound variables and truth sets, set-builder notation and universe of discourse, operations on sets (intersection/union/difference/symmetric difference), Venn diagrams, and the conditional connective with its truth table and equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: distinguish_statements_vs_names_for_objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish expressions that are mathematical statements from expressions that are names for mathematical objects (e.g., {x | P(x)} is not a statement but a name for a set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: {x | P(x)} is a set-name, not a statement. Use elementhood expressions (y ∈ {x | P(x)}) when you want to assert a statement about an object. Example: y ∈ {x | P(x)} means the same thing as P(y).

rubrics_metrics.name: identify_free_and_bound_variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which variables in a formula are free and which are bound; free variables make the statement's truth depend on their values while bound variables do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze expressions step-by-step to see which variables are quantified or occur inside set-builder bindings. Examples: in 'a+b ∉ {x | x is an even number}', a and b are free while x is bound; in nested set expressions trace inner bindings to find free variables. If there are no free variables, the statement has a fixed truth value.

rubrics_metrics.name: truth_set_definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth set of a statement P(x) (with one free variable x) is Truth set of P(x) = {x | P(x)} — the set of all values of x that make P(x) true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth sets to capture exactly which values satisfy P(x). If A is the truth set of P(x), then y ∈ A iff P(y). Note: the chapter limits the definition to single-variable statements here; multi-variable truth sets are discussed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: universe_of_discourse_and_explicit_notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the universe of discourse U when variables are intended to range over a particular set; use {x ∈ U | P(x)} to indicate membership tests restricted to U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of universe affects the truth set. Example: {x ∈ R | x^2 < 9} = reals between -3 and 3, while {x ∈ Z | x^2 < 9} = {-2,-1,0,1,2}. The notation can also be used to temporarily restrict attention to a part of the universe (e.g., positive reals).

rubrics_metrics.name: common_universes_and_notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Convenient standard names for common universes: R = reals, Q = rationals, Z = integers, N = natural numbers; superscripts +/− indicate positive/negative subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these symbols for compactness (e.g., R+ = {x | x is a positive real}). Note that conventions like whether 0 ∈ N may vary by text; this book includes 0 in N.

rubrics_metrics.name: interpret_elementhood_tests_as_statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that set-builder definitions use elementhood tests; the defining phrase P(x) in {x | P(x)} is an assertion about membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating between 'x ∈ {x | P(x)}' and 'P(x)' is routine and useful when manipulating sets and logical statements. Use this to relate sets to logical formulas when deriving identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: distinguish_elements_vs_sets_notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep straight the difference between an element and a singleton set: e.g., 2 is not the same as {2}; similarly ∅ (empty set) is not the same as {∅}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct notation: empty set is ∅ = {}; the set whose only element is ∅ is {∅}. Correctness of statements like '2 ∈ {2}' versus '2 ∈ 2' matters for logical form and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: definitions_of_set_operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal definitions: intersection A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}, union A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}, difference A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the words 'and/or/not' in these definitions as logical connectives in elementhood tests. Use these definitions to compute examples and to translate set expressions into propositional formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: inclusive_or_convention
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, the word 'or' is interpreted as inclusive or: x ∈ A ∪ B means x ∈ A or x ∈ B or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about unions, include elements that belong to both sets. This convention affects identities and Venn-diagram shading.

rubrics_metrics.name: symmetric_difference_and_identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetric difference A Δ B (denoted A A B in text) is the set of elements in either A or B but not both: A Δ B = (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Venn diagrams to visualize symmetric difference; the identity holds for all sets A and B and is often used in proofs and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: relationship_between_set_ops_and_logical_connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Map operations on sets to logical connectives when sets are truth sets: intersection ↔ conjunction (∩ ↔ ∧), union ↔ disjunction (∪ ↔ ∨), difference ↔ conjunction with negation (A \ B corresponds to P ∧ ¬Q for elementhood tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A and B are truth sets of P(x) and Q(x), then A ∩ B is truth set of P(x) ∧ Q(x), A ∪ B corresponds to P(x) ∨ Q(x), and U \ A corresponds to ¬P(x) (relative complement). Do not attempt to apply logical connectives directly to sets (expressions like A ∧ B are meaningless).

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_venn_diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sets and their combinations graphically: rectangle = universe U, circles = sets; shaded regions illustrate intersections, unions, differences, and other combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venn diagrams are helpful to see identities and disjointness, verify equalities (e.g., (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B) and (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) look the same), and reason about subset/disjoint relations. Note: overlapping-circle Venn diagrams are standard for up to three sets; for four or more sets other shapes are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: subset_and_disjointness_definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: A is a subset of B (A ⊂ B) if every element of A is in B; A and B are disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elementhood logic or Venn diagrams to verify subset or disjoint relations. Example: if A ⊂ B then draw A inside B; if A ∩ C = ∅ they do not overlap in Venn diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: proving_set_identities_via_logical_equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove set equalities, write 'x ∈ (set expression)' as a logical formula and use logical equivalences to transform one side into the other; sets with identical elementhood statements are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is illustrated repeatedly: e.g., show x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C) ⇔ x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) to derive distributivity. Alternatively, verify with Venn diagrams or truth tables where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: standard_set_identities_and_distributive_laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard identities: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C); A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C); A \ (B ∩ C) = (A \ B) ∪ (A \ C); A \ (B ∪ C) = (A \ B) ∩ (A \ C), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify via elementwise logical equivalences or Venn diagrams. Use De Morgan's laws and distributive laws of propositional logic as needed when translating between set and propositional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: identity_and_disjointness_checks_by_element_logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether two sets are always equal, one is subset of another, or they are disjoint by deriving the logical form of x ∈ each set and testing equivalence/contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show (A ∩ B) ∩ (A \ B) corresponds to (x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B) ∧ (x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B), which is a contradiction, hence (A ∩ B) ∩ (A \ B) = ∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: conditional_connective_truth_table
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional connective P → Q has truth table: (P,Q) = (F,F)→T, (F,T)→T, (T,F)→F, (T,T)→T — only false when P true and Q false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truth table is justified by examples like 'If x>2 then x^2>4' which is true for all x; analyze all possible truth-values of P(x) and Q(x) to force the table entries. Use this table to analyze conditional arguments and formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: equivalences_involving_conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalences: P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q, and also equivalent to ¬(P ∧ ¬Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these equivalences to translate conditionals into disjunction/negation forms for proofs and manipulations. Examples: teacher's warning 'You won't neglect your homework, or you'll fail' maps to ¬P ∨ Q ≡ P → Q in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_truth_tables_to_test_argument_validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use truth tables to test validity of arguments involving conditionals (e.g., modus ponens: from P → Q and P infer Q is valid because in all rows where premises true the conclusion is true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the table for premises and conclusion; check rows where all premises are true to see if conclusion is true in those rows (Figure 4 illustration). Changing the conditional truth table would lead to incorrect validity results, so the standard table must be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: logical_equivalence_transformations_and_tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply propositional logic equivalences (De Morgan, double negation, distributive laws) to transform and relate logical formulas and corresponding set expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: derive P ∨ Q ≡ ¬P → Q via double negation and substitution; derive set-theoretic distributivity from logical distributivity. Use these tools both to simplify formulas and to prove set identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: anti_patterns_and_meaningless_expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid combining syntactic categories incorrectly: do not write expressions that mix set operators with logical connectives improperly (e.g., A ∧ B or P(x) ∩ Q(x) are meaningless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ensure that logical connectives combine statements and set operations combine sets (or work with truth sets to translate between the two). When in doubt, translate to the form 'x ∈ ...' and examine the resulting propositional structure.
